title: Search Beyond What Can Be Taught: Evolving the Knowledge Boundary in Agentic Visual Generation
hook: Ask an image generator for a real but obscure or brand-new entity, and it'll confidently draw the wrong thing. A new benchmark shows how bad that gets — and how to teach it to search instead.
key_points: Frontier visual generators fabricate confidently when asked about things outside their training data — new characters, trending entities, events after their cutoff.
New benchmark SearchGen-Bench (20,839 prompts, 12 failure categories, 22 domains) shows frontier open generators score only 21-28/100 — a gap invisible to existing benchmarks.
Naive fix (bolt on retrieval) backfires: it retrieves indiscriminately and injects noise into prompts the generator already handles fine on its own.
The real issue is a generator-specific 'knowledge boundary' — what it already knows vs. what needs external context — that's hard to specify up front.
A teach-then-search co-training recipe lets the generator discover that boundary itself, giving monotonic improvement even in a minimal version.
Authors release the benchmark, prompts, and a pre-executed search corpus (SearchGen-Corpus-1M) as a reproducible, replayable harness.
content_html: Ask a state-of-the-art image generator to draw a specific, real but obscure entity — a new character, a trending person, something that happened after its training cutoff — and it won't say "I don't know." It will confidently draw something plausible and wrong. This paper, led by Wenhu Chen's group, measures exactly how bad that gets and proposes a fix.
extra_html:
The authors built SearchGen-Bench, a benchmark of 20,839 prompts spanning twelve failure categories and twenty-two domains specifically targeting this "world-knowledge bottleneck." Frontier open visual generators score only 21 to 28 out of 100 on it — a roughly 40-point collapse that existing benchmarks don't surface at all, since they don't test knowledge the generator was never trained on.

The obvious fix — bolt on a search tool — doesn't just work out of the box: naive retrieval grabs results indiscriminately, injecting noise into prompts the generator could already handle unaided. The real problem is that every generator has its own, evolving "knowledge boundary" between what it has internalized and what it needs external context for, and that boundary is hard to specify in advance. The authors show it's learnable instead, via a teach-then-search co-training recipe: even a minimal version produces monotonic improvement, which they frame as a first step toward visual generators that keep improving by learning when to trust themselves and when to search. The full benchmark, prompt set, and a pre-executed SearchGen-Corpus-1M are released as a reproducible harness.

related.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
related.hook: Why force a model to memorize everything? RAG lets it look things up — fetch relevant documents, then answer from that evidence instead of frozen weights alone.

related.title: Qwen-Image-2.0-RL: RLHF for a Diffusion Model
related.hook: Qwen's team applied RLHF and on-policy distillation to a text-to-image diffusion model — the same post-training playbook that shaped chat models, now tuning image generation and editing.

flashcards.prompt: What is the 'world-knowledge bottleneck' this paper identifies in visual generators?
flashcards.back_html: Generators are trained on fixed corpora, but the visual world is open-ended — so they confidently fabricate images for new entities, trending characters, or post-cutoff events instead of admitting they don't know.

flashcards.prompt: Why does naive retrieval-augmented generation fail for visual generators, per this paper?

choices.text: It retrieves indiscriminately, injecting noise into prompts the generator could already handle on its own
Search tools are too slow to ever use at inference time
Retrieved images are always lower resolution than generated ones

flashcards.explanation_html: Naive search doesn't discriminate between prompts that need external context and ones the generator already knows how to handle, so it adds noise rather than help.

flashcards.prompt: How does the teach-then-search co-training recipe address the knowledge boundary problem?
flashcards.back_html: Instead of specifying the boundary between internal knowledge and needed external context by hand, it lets the generator learn that boundary through co-training, producing monotonic improvement even in a minimal version.
